batchName: Late Republic: Caesar's Civil War and the Ides of March (49-44 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar's Civil War and the Ides of March (49-44 BCE)

questions.question: Which Pharsalus casualty figures come from Caesar's own claims? (select all that apply)
options: 200 of his own men lost
1,200 of his own men lost
60,000 enemy killed
1,000 of his own men lost
6,000 enemy killed
10,000 enemy killed
questions.explanation: Caesar claimed to have lost 200 men and killed 60,000. Another ancient historian gives the likelier figures of 1,200 and 6,000.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar claimed to have lost 200 men and killed 60,000; another ancient historian gives a likelier 1,200 and 6,000.

questions.question: How long did Caesar hold the dictatorship he took in December 49 BC before resigning it?
options: Seventy-two days
One year
Three months
Six months
Eleven days
Fifty days
questions.explanation: Caesar ran elections, won a second consulship, and resigned after just eleven days before setting off after Pompey.
questions.sourceQuote: He ran elections, won a second consulship, and resigned the dictatorship after just eleven days before setting off after Pompey.

questions.question: How do historians view the civil war's role in the fall of the Republic? (select all that apply)
options: A war forced on Rome by a Parthian invasion
A plan Caesar had designed from the very start
A struggle provoked mainly by Cleopatra
A symptom of a Republic already unable to reform
The blow that broke the Republic, triggered by miscalculation
A brief crisis the Republic easily survived
questions.explanation: Some historians see the war as the blow that broke the Republic, triggered by miscalculation rather than design. Others see it as a symptom of a Republic already unable to reform itself.
questions.sourceQuote: Others call it a symptom of a Republic already unable to reform itself.

questions.question: How did Caesar settle Egypt's throne after defeating the Egyptians?
options: Egypt was made a Roman province
Cleopatra ruled alone as sole queen
The boy king was restored under Roman guard
Cleopatra's infant son was named king
The regent ruled until a new king came of age
Cleopatra became queen alongside a younger brother
questions.explanation: Caesar made Cleopatra queen with a younger brother and cruised the Nile with her for three months. In 47 BC she bore a son who carried the Caesar name.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar made Cleopatra queen alongside a younger brother and cruised the Nile with her for three months.

questions.question: Caesar's last words are disputed. Which versions do ancient writers report? (select all that apply)
options: He spoke no last words at all
"Avenge me, Antony!" in Greek
"The die is cast" spoken in Latin
"Et tu, Brute?" spoken in Latin
"Jupiter alone is king" in Latin
"You too, child?" spoken in Greek
questions.explanation: Some ancient writers say Caesar said nothing; others report "You too, child?" in Greek. One says he covered his face on seeing Brutus.
questions.sourceQuote: Some ancient writers say he spoke none; others report "You too, child?" in Greek.

questions.question: What happened to Pompey's elder son after the battle of Munda?
options: He was pardoned by Caesar
He drowned fleeing the battle
He stabbed himself at Utica
He fled to Egypt
He joined the plot against Caesar
He was caught and beheaded
questions.explanation: Caesar won at Munda, losing around 1,000 men, and Pompey's elder son was caught and beheaded. One ancient writer says Caesar fought there for his life for the first time.
questions.sourceQuote: He won, losing around 1,000 men, and Pompey's elder son was caught and beheaded.

questions.question: Which ancient claim about Caesar's motives for war do modern historians doubt?
options: That the Senate voted 370 to 22
That the Senate passed its final decree
That pro-Caesar tribunes fled to him
That gang violence engulfed Rome
That he feared prosecution if he disarmed
That he wanted a second consulship
questions.explanation: Modern historians doubt that fear of prosecution drove Caesar. Pride on both sides seems to have tipped Rome into war.
questions.sourceQuote: Modern historians doubt ancient claims that he feared prosecution.

questions.question: According to one ancient writer, why did Caesar's veterans charge at Thapsus before he gave the order?
options: He was still landing his troops
He had been wounded by an elephant
He was sacrificing for good omens
He had fallen from his horse
He was having an epileptic fit
He was negotiating with the Numidian king
questions.explanation: One ancient writer says Caesar was having an epileptic fit. The battle was lopsided: some 10,000 Pompeians died against about 50 of Caesar's men.
questions.sourceQuote: At Thapsus, in modern Tunisia, in 46 BC, Caesar's veterans charged before he gave the order; one ancient writer says he was having an epileptic fit.

questions.question: Of the three incidents ancient writers saw as the last straws against Caesar, which came last?
options: Mark Antony offering a diadem at the Lupercalia
Some in a crowd hailing Caesar as king
Two tribunes being stripped of office
Caesar celebrating triumphs with 72 lictors
Caesar staying seated before a Senate delegation
A diadem appearing on Caesar's statue
questions.explanation: The Lupercalia, a February festival, came after the January 44 BC episode of the statue's diadem and the cries of "rex". Antony offered the diadem twice.
questions.sourceQuote: Third, at the Lupercalia, a February festival, Mark Antony, Caesar's loyal lieutenant and fellow consul, twice placed a diadem on his head.

questions.question: What is notable about Caesar's own account of the crossing of the Rubicon?
options: It quotes a Greek poet
It never mentions the river at all
It credits Mark Antony with the idea
It dates the crossing to 9 March
It records "the die is cast"
It describes a bad omen at the river
questions.explanation: Caesar's own account never mentions the Rubicon. The famous lines come from other ancient writers, who disagree over what he said.
questions.sourceQuote: Another ancient writer says he quoted a Greek poet instead, and Caesar's own account never mentions the river at all.
